Concomitant lower motor neuron findings in the hands — weakness, absent reflexes, and fasciculations — point to involvement of anterior horn cells at the cervical enlargement. MRI confirms a syrinx spanning the cervical to upper thoracic cord, which explains both the sensory cape distribution and the LMN signs. The delayed onset of symptoms years after a motor vehicle accident is characteristic of post‑traumatic syringomyelia. Diabetes-related peripheral neuropathy and ALS are less consistent: diabetic neuropathy is typically symmetric distal sensory loss (not dissociated or “cape” distribution), and ALS usually preserves sensation and shows upper motor neuron signs; neither explains the syrinx seen on imaging. Therefore the most likely diagnosis is a post‑traumatic syringomyelia causing central cord syndrome at the cervical level.

DIAGNOSIS: Syringomyelia (post‑traumatic) causing central cervical cord syndrome.
